title: Lahāinā Strong Candidate Forum: General Election | 2026

recap.headline: Lahaina Strong holds general election forum for Maui mayor and six County Council seats
recap.in_60_seconds: Lahaina Strong held a general election candidate forum outdoors at a Lahaina canoe club site, with a civic media partner and community moderators from local organizations. Each race had its own panel with up to four questions. Candidates had 90 seconds per answer and the mayor had three minutes, with timekeeper lights and no rebuttals or follow-ups. Eleven candidates took part across the Maui County mayor race and six County Council races, several opponents did not attend, and one Upcountry candidate sent a video message. Questions covered fire recovery, housing, water, wildfire and energy resilience, tourism, immigrant access to services, houselessness, development and council independence.
recap.moderated_by: Community moderators from local organizations, including Save Honolua Coalition and Lahaina Community Land Trust, and a civic media journalist

questions.question: After the fires you prioritized residents and housing in Lahaina's recovery; how did you decide what to prioritize, how have those priorities shifted, and what would you prioritize if reelected?

answers.summary: Said the administration listened to the community and prioritized owner-occupants to keep residents from leaving, aiming to speed housing rebuilding. Said commercial rebuilding faced water, wastewater and infrastructure repairs but also received expedited permitting and third-party review. Said he does not regret prioritizing local residents, since businesses need workers and workers need housing.

questions.question: Where has your administration made housing truly affordable for local families, where has it fallen short, and what would you focus on if reelected?

answers.summary: Said affordable housing rose 190% in three and a half years, from about 90 homes a year to 293, using county-owned land and county infrastructure, citing the rebuilt 89 units at Kayulu O Kuohi in Lahina. Said the county gives 20% of its GET to Hawaiian Homelands for infrastructure. Plans 5,000 more homes in four years, 3,000 affordable.

questions.question: Where does the proposed purchase of Maui Land & Pineapple's West Maui water system stand, what has changed since July, and how have you responded to concerns about who will benefit most?

answers.summary: Said we've already purchased portions of three of the four water systems, and that acquiring Maui Land and Pine's would take West Maui drinking water from 45% to 93%. Said negotiation continues with no appraisal yet, nothing is finalized, the county council must approve, and the goal is to benefit the community, not enrich a company.

questions.question: Beyond better emergency response, what is the biggest systemic change Maui needs to become more resilient over the long term, and how would you encourage it if reelected?

answers.summary: Said the first step is reducing fuel loads in high-risk corridors, citing debris cleared from 42 acres. Said the emergency management office has 31 approved positions and AI cameras, with 29 new firefighters, water tankers in every station, and stations coming in Olawalu and Hayeku. Said to prepare for the disaster not yet had.

questions.question: Why do you believe you have earned the opportunity to represent West Maui: for the challenger, what motivated you and what needs to change; for the incumbent, what are you most proud of and why do you deserve another term?

answers.summary: Said he wants to repurpose his life rather than retire, continuing to give back after 39 years living here. Cited involvement with every school board and team his children played on, and the Lahina Luna High School Foundation board, which secured land from the Department of Education and built a new stadium with private donations.

Named the post-fire insurance gap pilot program, extended beyond one rebuilt complex to other households, as her proudest accomplishment. Said first-year funding of $300,000 per household could bring 10 families home, it has been funded every year since, and it lets the land trust, lenders and builders partner. Said she has more legislation planned to make housing more affordable.

questions.question: If elected, what is one specific policy you would prioritize introducing in your term, and why?

answers.summary: Said she is working on three bills regulating the county's use of license plate readers and technologies such as facial recognition, one of which moved out of committee. Said people want full transparency on how the technology is used, its purpose and who has access, and that the conversation will continue into the next term.

Proposed green zones around the city, citing many fires since sugarce ceased production in 1999, 20 homes lost in 2018, and the whole town burning in 2023. Proposed diverting R1 recycled water, millions of gallons every day now dumped in injection wells, back down into town.

questions.question: If funding allowed R-1 recycled water expansion in only one direction, north toward businesses and resorts or south toward Lahaina for fire mitigation and restoration, which would you prioritize and why?

answers.summary: Said after $4 billion in losses the issue is not money and both directions should happen at the same time so the town never burns again. Compared a $142 million school rebuild cost with $18 million for a Kīhei school 30 years ago, and said the work is necessary.

Said she is committed to the county funding the south line to green around Lahina Town, creating a green buffer that would make a real difference in subsequent fire seasons. Said she is open to Mr. Yai building a transmission line north and taking whatever excess water there is, since she would rather not dump water into injection wells.

questions.question: What specific investments or solutions would you prioritize to make West Maui's energy system more reliable and resilient while balancing environmental impacts?

answers.summary: Proposed studying the cost of undergrounding the transmission line into West Maui. Said if the utility adds backup generation in one area, the county should add backup sites farther away and educate residents on where to go during outages, so preparation becomes a drill for any disaster.

Said power outages once were very few and far between but now happen too frequently, and when power goes out residents have no way of contacting fire, police or ambulances. Said we at least need some type of emergency backup system and that the situation with Hawaiʻi Electric must be fixed.

questions.question: Looking at your record representing East Maui, what are you most proud of accomplishing, and why do you believe you have earned another term?

answers.summary: Cited promoting water and food security, including through the county Department of Agriculture, and keiki safety through non-chemical spraying in county parks near the ocean and along county roads.

questions.question: With the future of East Maui's water system still unresolved, what would you do next to secure public control and ensure East Maui streams are sustained for current and future generations?

answers.summary: Thanked Mayor Bon and those who attended the BLNR meeting where a long-term lease was denied, and hopes to work with the state to manage the waterways. Said public trust water should be used for agriculture and food security, not more luxury homes. Said he supported funding to acquire the Olawalu system.

questions.question: How would you make East Maui's tourism economy more regenerative and less harmful, what specific changes have you made in office, and what would you prioritize if reelected?

answers.summary: Said he is happy to host visitor traffic in East Maui while the Lahina rebuild takes several more years, noting construction and utility vehicles are coming to West Maui. Suggested those who haven't driven the road to Hana take a tour, which takes at least 50 cars off the road, and urged residents to drive into town earlier, return later, and avoid road rage.

questions.question: If reelected, what is the one specific policy you would prioritize introducing in your next term, and why?

answers.summary: Said policy success comes from working with the community. Said after recent storms he has heard calls to slow further development and invest in infrastructure such as evacuation routes and drainage moving water mauka to mākaʻi, while keeping the economy going and people safe.

questions.question: With the Wailuku-Waiheʻe-Waikapū seat open, what changes can voters expect if you are elected, and why should Maui County voters choose you?

answers.summary: Said he would meet with county department directors about budget and staffing challenges to make government more productive. Said his Department of Transportation airports work reworked its budget to fund airport infrastructure, and county savings should go toward Maui infrastructure.

Said she ran because of the upcoming Central Maui community plan, last changed about 30 years ago, after working on the South Maui plan on the planning commission. Said her main priority is getting Wailuku residents, including younger people, involved and heard on changes.

questions.question: With both campaigns supported by money from powerful groups that benefit from the status quo, do you see yourself as more of a change candidate or a status quo candidate, and what evidence can you point to?

answers.summary: Said the Carpenters Union supported her primary campaign through its Partners for Democracy program, help she needed after filing with a two-week-old baby. Said her planning commission record shows she weighs each issue separately with community input and does not choose sides.

Said his contributions reflect 20 years at Hawaiian Airlines and 20 years with the airports division. Said overseeing airport police, fire and maintenance taught him how to make changes, and he would act as the ninth member rather than part of a five-four split, deciding for the people and the next generation.

questions.question: What would you do to make county and state services safe for immigrant families to access, and would you support a policy limiting data sharing with federal immigration authorities?

answers.summary: Proposed educational workshops and programs to help immigrant communities facing language barriers get help. Said Maui has good local police and FBI and does not need ICE here, which he said could remove sex, drug and human traffickers but should otherwise leave.

Said she would support protecting people, who should never be scared to get help in emergencies. Described organizing Kīpuka Maui after the fires, giving a donated check straight to people who couldn't access services, and helping a translation group get $200,000 from private donors.

questions.question: Given limited water, infrastructure and budget, what types of housing would you prioritize, which would you deprioritize, and how would you make that happen on the council?

answers.summary: Said the community should look back at how people who lived here for thousands of years managed resources, prioritizing where local people benefit most. Proposed changing infrastructure to use R1 water and educating kiki to understand water's importance and become good resource managers.

Said workforce housing should be prioritized so West Maui residents can live and work on that side, citing the Capalua Mahina project's idle site, stalled partly by water. Said the airport's water scalping project takes 80,000 to 100,000 gallons a day and converts it to R1 water; subdivisions should recycle water with developers paying.

questions.question: What keeps you motivated to seek elected office, and why is this the right moment for voters to choose you?

answers.summary: Said her philosophy is that if we are not at the table, we are on the menu, and community testimony often goes unheeded. Said she wants to be the community's voice, accepts no PAC or construction money, and has given back through community and military service.

Said his interest in public service began as a student at Commment School's Maui during the broken trust scandal and the John Doe KS lawsuit, a challenge to the Hawaiian preference policy, when he stood on the side of the road wearing red. Said the legislative platform offers an unparalleled opportunity to enact change.

questions.question: If elected, what would be your strategy for getting houseless people into stable permanent housing, and how would you measure whether it is working?

answers.summary: Said after the fires he led county health and social services efforts and found no coherent county houselessness policy. Said he is pushing for short- and medium-term goals with the new human concerns director, and supports mental health services, drug abuse enforcement and social services to keep people from becoming houseless.

Said she has worked as a houseless advocate for six years since the Kanahā relocation. Proposed using the governor's proclamation to build more shelters and housing, noting only one Central Maui shelter remains after the fires. Said causes include cost of living, as a $16 minimum wage cannot cover a $1.5 million home.

questions.question: With many Maui water systems still privately controlled, what should come next for Maui's water systems, and what have you done or would you do on the council to get there?

answers.summary: Supports the mayor purchasing as much of the private water systems as possible, saying water is a public trust that belongs in the hands of the people who live here, for basic substance and growing food, not corporate hands. Said she doesn't believe the fires would have happened with public control.

Agrees water systems should be in public hands and said he has supported every administration proposal to acquire water source, transmission and storage. Said his criticism has been of contract details, which council members must scrutinize for the public good.

questions.question: Can you point to a specific time you broke publicly with allies you normally work alongside, and how would you bring that independence to the council?

answers.summary: Said they have a proven track record of independence, citing a number of votes against colleagues, including the Department of Human Concerns director confirmation, where they didn't think she met the one-year residency requirement. Said they reached out early to the mayor, met four times with corporation council, and shared questions in advance because how they disagree matters.

Said she supported Bill 9, which her opponent did not, and does not support Bill 18 or Bill 88. Said council members should disagree respectfully and seek clarification to understand each other, and she would listen to the community first.

questions.question: Make your case to voters: for the challenger, what motivated you and what needs to change in how the district is represented; for the incumbent, what are you most proud of and why do you deserve another term?

answers.summary: Said she ran because of issues that have not been addressed in the decade she has lived on the island, including poisoning of crops and land that causes people immune problems, and wastewater infrastructure. Said she is not taking support from dark money developers and packs, and wants to advocate for what the community is asking for.

Said more options are better and supports everyone who runs. Said, as chair of the housing and land use committee, the balance sought with fellow council members is a point of pride despite a heavy split, along with making a dent in the housing market to keep local people home.

questions.question: What is your position on the proposed Pāʻia developments that residents have raised concerns about, and how would you address concerns about safety, infrastructure, water, affordability and the town's character?

answers.summary: Said Pāʻia's demographics have changed and it has had no affordable housing project in 30 years. Supports housing there and would sacrifice some of the town's look so local people can buy, noting her grandmother's $27,000 home is now about $1.7 million. Said developers must find water and work continues on evacuation routes and traffic.

Said it is not black or white whether she is for or against these developments, and she wants local input on any future project. Said development can take Maui toward an "ʻAʻahu 2.0", and she would look at individual projects to see how they benefit the community.

questions.question: What specific housing policies would you introduce or prioritize to serve local working-class families and help future generations afford to stay?

answers.summary: Supports the county developing on land it owns to control sale and rental prices. Said she also wants to help people living on the streets, citing sweeps against residents, including generational Hawaiians, who cannot afford housing.

Said the EC PA project includes for-purchase gap group homes, above affordable but below market, with a reserve system for professionals, firemen and police officers. Said interest rates are killing us, supports the Lahina Community Trust and more community land trusts, and noted extended deed restrictions.

questions.question: Whose voices are overrepresented in Maui County decision-making, whose are left out, and what would you do to change that?

answers.summary: Said she is not afraid of tough conversations. Said testimony comes mostly from people paid to be in chambers or retirees, a chronic 10, and she wants to make participation more comfortable and hear more from everyday local working people, including parents and her peers.

Said elders are overrepresented while her generation, Gen Z, feels defeated and unheard, unable to achieve what earlier generations could, such as buying homes. Said she wants her generation to speak out more.

questions.question: After losing the last South Maui election by fewer than 100 votes, what motivated you to run again, and what needs to change about how South Maui is represented?

answers.summary: Said she first ran in 2016 at community urging over an unwanted mega mall and planned to serve three terms. Said the wetland overlay map, wetland funding and youth council stopped after she left while the current majority approved luxury development, and that people need representation.

questions.question: What specific changes would you champion in how Maui County manages land and water to reduce wildfire risk, restore healthy landscapes and better protect communities?

answers.summary: Proposed county funding for volunteer-run resilience hubs, started during her council tenure, so they can sustain generators and stored water and blankets for evacuees. Said productive agricultural land helps with fire risk, citing a fire that stopped at the edge of a sunflower field she works on.

questions.question: What specific policies would you prioritize introducing to help Maui build a more diversified, regenerative economy beyond tourism and real estate?

answers.summary: Said her council majority shifted tourism money to agriculture, and she wants to continue and increase agriculture micro grants for food security. Cited film productions during COVID that followed their own protocols and gave 2% back to the community, and called for focus on health, education and agriculture.

questions.question: If elected, what specific differences should South Maui residents expect in the final South Maui community plan, and what would you fight to include, remove or change?

answers.summary: Thanked Council Member Tamara Palolton for slowing down the South Maui community plan and for in-person testimony in Kīhei. Said there isn't enough water for all 7,000 units, which she called luxury development, and that affordable housing, agriculture and wastewater should come first.
